claims.claim: The published chapter abstract states the style relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel and Tolkien's Beowulf translation, with archaic verb forms, high-frequency along/among/dark/deep/fell/great/long, and collocations mixing archaic and modern registers.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (Springer chapter abstract)
claims.quote: several centuries' worth of linguistic developments

claims.claim: Furkó analyses discourse-pragmatic devices in The Hobbit as authentication strategies of its storytelling voice.
claims.source: Furkó 2020, 'Discourse Markers and Their Translation in Literary Discourse' (Springer chapter abstract)

claims.claim: Lobdell argues the architecture and narrative style of the Edwardian adventure story (King Solomon's Mines, The Lost World) underlie The Hobbit and LOTR.
claims.source: Lobdell, The World of the Rings (Internet Archive record)

claims.claim: Lewis's 1954 review says the names alone are a feast, sorted by sound into homely (Michel Delving), kingly (Boromir, Elendil) and loathsome (Gollum).
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, The Gods Return to Earth (1954; theonering.com reprint)
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.feature: free indirect discourse in crisis; Gothic register
claims.claim: Frodo's temptation in the barrow is rendered in free indirect discourse, and the grave-goods details give the chapter a Gothic antiquarian register distinct from the novel's vernacular voice.
claims.source: Abigail Nussbaum, The Great Tolkien Reread: Fog on the Barrow-Downs (2026-03-10)
claims.quote: He thought of himself running free over the grass
claims.page: The Great Tolkien Reread: Fog on the Barrow-Downs
routeHints: Google Books search-inside id=9uAsEAAAQBAJ for "free indirect" and "focaliz"

claims.claim: Nearly all alliterative verse in LotR belongs to the Rohirrim; it front-loads stress on consonant clusters rather than end-rhyme, and the prose following 'Arise, arise' is full of battle-fury.
